sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case involves Idaho's law excluding students whose biological sex is male from women's sports teams. The dispute centers on whether that exclusion counts as a sex classification that the Constitution's Equal Protection Clause requires courts to examine closely.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: A lower court blocked Idaho's law while the case moved forward. The state appealed, and the Supreme Court heard argument on the dispute.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Idaho and its supporters argue the state may separate sports teams by sex because biological differences like size, muscle mass, and lung capacity matter in athletics. They say the state may apply that rule to students who identify as female but were born male.

The students challenging the law argue Idaho concedes it draws a sex-based line by excluding all students born male from women's teams. They say such classifications demand close judicial review to confirm they rest on evidence rather than assumptions.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Idaho's lawyer argued that sex correlates strongly with athletic advantages and that male athletes have injured female athletes in many sports. He said states may apply a valid sex-based team rule to biological males who identify as female.

The challengers' lawyer argued that the law categorically excludes an entire group of students from women's teams. He agreed that if the excluded group is large enough, the exclusion may fail constitutional review on its face.

And Asked whether the law's treatment of one individual fits that framework. The justice also noted that sex classifications in sports themselves were not being challenged in this case.
